n16-1.name: Priam’s Birdwing
n16-1.range: Moluccas to New Guinea and northern Australia
facts: The first birdwing ever described, named by Linnaeus in 1758 after Priam, king of Troy. He gave the great swallowtails the names of Trojan heroes.
The male’s green is structural colour, not pigment: microscopic ridges on the scales scatter light. The engraver could only approximate it with paint.
Females are larger, brown and cream, and were long thought to be a different species.
Caterpillars feed on poisonous Dutchman’s pipe vines and carry the toxin into adulthood, so birds learn to leave the adults alone.

Lucas, 1835: “This butterfly, remarkable for the beauty of its colours and for its size, is without doubt one of the finest of its genus, and it was to this species that Linnaeus gave the epithet of Augustus. The forewings are oval, entire, of a matt velvet black above, with two bands of golden green, curved and narrow, one running along the costa and the other along the whole of the opposite edge.”
Named by Linnaeus for Priam, king of Troy. In his 1758 system the largest swallowtails were the Trojans, the Equites Trojani, and their names still ring of the Iliad.
n16-1.caption: g. Ornithoptera Priamus ♂, île d’Amboine

n18-1.name: Golden Birdwing
facts: A birdwing of the Philippines, where it flies in forest clearings and along rivers; the male's hindwings are the colour of old gold, the female's are duller and larger.
Like all birdwings its caterpillars feed on Aristolochia vines and take up their poisons, and every species of the genus is listed under the international trade convention CITES.
Boisduval named it only in 1836, so Lucas was among the first to picture it, and he used Cramer's older name Amphrisius on the plate.
Named for Rhadamanthus, the Cretan lawgiver who became a judge of the dead. Boisduval gave the name in 1836; Lucas printed it the year the species was described.

n18-2.name: Androgeus Swallowtail
facts: A common swallowtail of the American tropics from Mexico to Argentina; the male is banded with yellow, the female is dark with blue on the hindwings and looks like a different insect.
Its caterpillars feed on citrus and on the prickly ash, Zanthoxylum, and are among the orange-grove pests of Brazil.
Named for Polycaon, a Spartan prince who became the first king of Messenia.

n20-1.name: Ulysses Butterfly
facts: The electric blue is structural, thrown back by ridges on the scales, and it flashes on and off as the butterfly beats its wings over the rainforest canopy of New Guinea and northern Queensland.
Males will dive at anything blue, including clothing, which is how collectors and photographers still lure them down from the trees.
The caterpillars feed on trees of the citrus family, especially Melicope, and the adult has become the emblem of tourism in tropical Queensland.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are velvet black above, with a patch of azure blue that turns violet or green according to the angle at which one examines it. This patch runs from the base of all four wings to beyond the middle, its hind edge scalloped, and near the front edge of the forewings there is a fairly large black dot, present in the female too.”
Named by Linnaeus for Ulysses, the wanderer of the Odyssey. The name has never changed, which is rare for a butterfly described in 1758.
One of the cattlehearts, Parides, named for the red heart-shaped spots many of them carry on the hindwing; this one flies in south-eastern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina.
Its caterpillars feed on Aristolochia, the pipevines, and the poisons they store make the adults distasteful to birds.
Named for Agave, daughter of Cadmus, who in her frenzy tore her own son Pentheus apart.

n22-2.name: Crimson Rose
n22-2.range: Lucas's specimen: Bengale, Coromandel, Ile d'Amboine
facts: A swallowtail of India and Sri Lanka whose caterpillars feed on Aristolochia and make it poisonous; birds learn to leave it alone, and the harmless female of the Common Mormon copies its pattern almost exactly.
It gathers in numbers to migrate across southern India, and dozens may roost together on a single bush at dusk.
Lucas's engraving shows the black forewings and crimson-spotted hindwings that give the English name; his caption adds Amboina, where it does not in fact occur.
Named for Hector, Troy's champion. A Trojan name from Linnaeus, given to a red-bodied swallowtail he placed among the Trojans.

n32-1.name: Common Bluebottle
facts: One of the fastest and most widespread swallowtails of Asia and Australia, a rapid flier that rarely settles except to drink at wet sand or puddles, often in company.
The caterpillars feed on camphor and cinnamon trees, so it thrives in cities where these are planted.
The pale band across the wings is blue-green in life; the engraver has caught its translucence, which comes from the band having almost no scales.
Named for Sarpedon, the Lycian king killed by Patroclus before the walls of Troy.

n32-2.name: Veined Jay
facts: A swallowtail of the forests of South-east Asia from Burma to Borneo and Java, one of the jays, Graphium, that gather in dozens to drink at riverbanks.
The dark veins that cross the pale patches, and give it its English name, are clear in Lucas's figure.
Named for Bathycles of Magnesia, the sculptor who made the throne of Apollo at Amyclae.

Lucas's Polymetus, from Brazil, has not yet been matched to a modern species with confidence; the plate shows a black cattleheart-like swallowtail with white forewing patches and rose-red hindwing bands.
Cramer described a Papilio Polymetus in 1782, and the figure is a fair copy of his; the name has since been treated as a form or synonym of one of the South American Parides.
Named for Polymetus; Cramer's coinage, from the Greek for much counsel.

n34-2.name: Common Clubtail
facts: The spatulate tails and the slow, drifting flight are the marks of this swallowtail from India to Java; it feeds on Aristolochia as a caterpillar and is left alone by birds as an adult.
The pale hindwing patches vary from white to yellow between regions, and the old name Coon comes from a Trojan in the Iliad, not from any resemblance.
Not a hero at all: Fabricius took the name from Coön, a Trojan warrior in the Iliad who wounded Agamemnon.
Lucas's Evander, from Brazil, awaits a confident modern identification; the plate shows a swallowtail of the cattleheart group with a red bar across the forewing and a red-spotted hindwing.
Godart gave the name in 1819; the figure was probably drawn from a specimen in the Paris museum, where Lucas worked.
Named for Evander, the Arcadian who settled on the Palatine before Rome was founded and welcomed Aeneas.

n36-2.name: Vertumnus Cattleheart
facts: A cattleheart of the Amazon and Guianas, black with a pink or red flash on the hindwing; males carry a fold of pale scent scales along the inner edge of the hindwing, which the engraver has shown as a white streak.
The caterpillars feed on pipevines, Aristolochia, and the whole group is poisonous to predators.
Named for Vertumnus, the Roman god of the changing seasons and of gardens.

n38-1.name: Yellow Kite
facts: A kite swallowtail of the Atlantic forest of Brazil, pale yellow with black bands and long tails; it has become rare as the coastal forest has been cleared and is now protected.
Lucas took the name from Hübner, who described it in the 1820s; the figure is one of the earliest coloured pictures of the species.
Named for Iphitus, whose bow Odysseus carried and used to slay the suitors.

n38-2.name: Pipevine Swallowtail
facts: The most important model for mimicry in North America: because its caterpillars feed on pipevines and make it poisonous, the dark female tiger swallowtail, the spicebush swallowtail, the black swallowtail and the red-spotted purple all copy its blue-black colours.
The caterpillars are black with orange spines and feed openly in groups; the adults are the only butterflies in the eastern United States with iridescent blue-green hindwings.
Pauquet drew this one from the side on a spray of its plant, the only such figure in the book; it is the one specimen that does not open its wings to the reader.
The name means lover of husband in Greek; Linnaeus gave it in 1771 to the pipevine swallowtail of North America.

n40-1.name: Orchard Swallowtail
facts: The largest butterfly commonly seen in Australian gardens, where it lays on cultivated citrus; the male is black and white, the female carries red and blue on the hindwing.
Donovan named it Erectheus in 1805, but Linnaeus had already described it as Aegeus, and that name stands.
New Holland, on Lucas's caption, was still the usual name for Australia in Paris in 1835.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are toothed, black, with whitish notches. The forewings carry a whitish, interrupted streak opposite the apex; the hindwings are crossed in the middle by a broad greyish-white band, sinuous on its outer side, ending at the anal angle in a blood-red lunule dusted with blue.”
Named for Erechtheus, the legendary king of Athens whose temple stands on the Acropolis.

n40-2.name: Lime Butterfly
n40-2.range: Lucas's specimen: Cap de Bonne Espérance
facts: The only tailless Papilio of its group and one of the most widespread swallowtails in the world, from Africa through Asia to Australia; its caterpillars are a pest of lime and orange trees.
It reached the Caribbean in 2004, probably with nursery citrus, and has since spread through the Greater Antilles.
Lucas's specimen came from the Cape of Good Hope; the African population is now often treated as a separate species, Papilio demodocus.
Named for Demoleus, a Greek slain by Aeneas in the Aeneid. Linnaeus placed the species among the Achivi, the Greek knights.

n50-1.name: Small Réunion Swallowtail
n50-1.range: Lucas's specimen: Ile de France, Bourbon
facts: Found only on the island of Réunion, Lucas's Île Bourbon, where it is now rare and protected; its caterpillars feed on native citrus relatives and on cultivated orange trees.
The two figures on this plate are the male and the female of one species: Boisduval's Disparilis, below, is the female, which is far more mottled than the male above.
Named for Phorbas, a hero of several Greek tales, among them the boxer who challenged travellers to Delphi.

n50-2.name: Small Réunion Swallowtail (female)
facts: This is the female of the butterfly above. Lucas followed Boisduval in treating it as a separate species, Disparilis, because the sexes look so different.
Female swallowtails are often duller than males, but in this Réunion endemic the contrast is unusually strong, with brown and yellow mottling in place of the male's green-blue.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are toothed, of a deep blackish brown above, with whitish notches. Towards the middle of the wing the male shows a large patch of fine blue-green, set transversely and divided in three by the veins, and near the apex of the same wings three more spots of the same colour.”

n52-1.name: Scarlet Mormon
facts: A giant swallowtail of the Moluccas and Sulawesi, among the largest Papilio in the world; the female shown here carries the scarlet on the hindwing that gives the English name.
The caterpillars feed on citrus and other rue-family trees, and the adults patrol forest edges with a slow, sailing flight.
Named for Deiphobus, son of Priam, who took Helen as his wife after Paris fell.

n54-1.name: Blue Mormon
facts: The second largest butterfly of India and Sri Lanka, velvet black with a wash of pale blue on the hindwings; in 2015 it was declared the state butterfly of Maharashtra.
It flies in the wet forests of the Western Ghats and is fond of Lantana and Ixora flowers; the caterpillars feed on citrus.
Named for Polymnestor, the Thracian king of Euripides' Hecuba, who murdered Priam's youngest son for his gold.

n54-2.name: Swift Peacock
facts: A swallowtail of the Indonesian islands whose green-blue sheen on a black ground is one of the most brilliant among the peacock swallowtails.
Lucas's Cochinchine is southern Vietnam; the species is in fact confined to Java, Bali and the islands eastward, so the locality was probably a dealer's guess.
Named for Peranthus; Fabricius's coinage, apparently from the Greek for around the flowers.

n56-1.name: Banded Swallowtail
facts: The one swallowtail that lays its eggs in a string: the female glues a chain of a dozen or more eggs to a leaf, and the caterpillars feed side by side in a row, an unusual habit in the family.
Lucas called it Cresphontes, a name that properly belongs to the North American giant swallowtail; his own synonym, Cramer's Demolion, is the correct one, and his Java is right.
The caterpillars feed on citrus relatives in the forests of Malaya, Sumatra and Java.

Lucas, 1835: “This species, of middling size, is sulphur white on both surfaces. The tip of the forewings is edged above by a broad arched black band, much widened at the apex, where it carries a dot of the ground colour; the hindwings have very blunt teeth and a fairly long yellowish spatulate tail, with three black spots towards the middle of the surface.”
Named for Cresphontes, a descendant of Heracles who won Messenia by lot when the Peloponnese was divided.

n56-2.name: Red Helen
facts: A large black swallowtail of the Asian forests from India to Japan, with a great white patch on each hindwing and a row of red crescents beneath; it is a strong flier that visits flowers in the forest canopy.
The caterpillars feed on wild citrus relatives, and the adults are commonly seen drinking at wet ground in the hills.
Named for Helenus, the seer-prince of Troy and twin of Cassandra.

n66-1.name: Mocker Swallowtail (male)
n66-1.range: Lucas's specimen: Côte occ. Afrique, Cap de Bonne-Espérance
facts: The male mocker swallowtail is the flying handkerchief of African forests, cream and black with tails; the females look nothing like him, and copy a dozen different poisonous butterflies instead.
This female mimicry, controlled by a single genetic switch with many forms, made the species a classic case study in evolutionary genetics in the twentieth century.
Lucas used Fabricius's name Brutus; Cramer's Merope, which Lucas cites, and Brown's Dardanus are the same butterfly, and Dardanus has priority.
Named for Brutus, the Roman who drove out the Tarquin kings. Fabricius named it in 1793.
This Brazilian Dardanus of Fabricius is not the African mocker swallowtail that now bears the name, but one of the South American cattlehearts; which one has not yet been settled.
The plate shows a black swallowtail with a red bar on the hindwing and pale spots at the forewing tip, and Lucas printed it between Brutus and Aeneas.
Named for Dardanus, the mythical founder of the Trojan line, from whom the Dardanelles take their name.
Parides aeneas is a cattleheart of the Amazon basin and the Guianas, black with a green or blue-green patch on the forewing and pink on the hindwing.
Linnaeus named it in 1758 for Aeneas, placing it among his Trojans; the caterpillars feed on pipevines and the adults are poisonous.
Named by Linnaeus for Aeneas, the Trojan prince who escaped the burning city to found the Roman line.

n68-1.name: Emerald-patched Cattleheart
facts: The brilliant green patch on the forewing is structural colour and shifts with the angle of view; males carry it, females do not.
It ranges from Mexico to the Amazon and is one of the most frequently seen cattlehearts at forest edges, where it feeds on pipevines as a caterpillar.
Lucas's Guyane is French Guiana, whose specimens reached Paris in quantity through the colonial administration.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are deep black above and crossed towards the middle by a band of greenish yellow, narrowed and broken into round spots near the apex of the forewings; the hindwings carry a row of lunules of the same colour parallel to the hind edge. These wings are very bluntly toothed, edged with white at the notches, and end in a black tail a little spatulate.”
Named for Sesostris, the legendary Egyptian conqueror of Herodotus, who is usually identified with the pharaohs Senusret.
Lucas's Dimas, from Brazil, awaits a confident identification; the figure shows a small black swallowtail with a green forewing flash and a broad red hindwing band, of the cattleheart group.
The name comes from Dymas, king of Phrygia in the Iliad.
Named for Dymas, king of Phrygia and father of Hecuba.
Godart's Nephalion is a Brazilian swallowtail of the cattleheart group; the plate shows black wings with a white forewing band and a red hindwing patch. Its modern identity has not yet been fixed.
Named for Nephalion, a son of Minos killed by Heracles at Paros.

n70-1.name: Fluminense Swallowtail
facts: One of the rarest swallowtails in the world, confined to a few coastal marshes near Rio de Janeiro where its pipevine grows; it was among the first Brazilian insects legally protected, in 1973.
The name Fluminense means of the river, and is the term for a native of the state of Rio de Janeiro.
Named for Ascanius, son of Aeneas, who founded Alba Longa.
Mimoides lysithous is a harmless swallowtail of south-eastern Brazil that copies the poisonous cattlehearts so closely, in several different forms, that it was long confused with them.
Lucas placed it beside Ascanius on the plate, and it is in fact a mimic of that very species in part of its range.
Named for Lysithous; Fabricius's coinage, of uncertain origin.

n80-1.name: Belus Swallowtail
facts: A gold-rim swallowtail of the American tropics, black with a greenish sheen and a band of yellow spots; like its relatives it feeds on pipevines and is poisonous.
Males of the genus Battus flutter their wings continuously while feeding at flowers, a habit that makes them easy to recognise in flight.
Named for Belus, the legendary king of Egypt or Tyre and father of Dido in the Aeneid.

n80-2.name: Polydamas Swallowtail
facts: The only tailless swallowtail in the eastern United States, where it reaches Florida and Texas; it ranges south to Argentina.
The caterpillars feed on pipevines and are gregarious when young; the adults visit lantana and other flowers with a nervous, fluttering flight.
Linnaeus named it in 1758; Lucas's figure shows the row of yellow spots along the wing margins and the pale spotting of the underside showing through.
Named by Linnaeus for Polydamas, the Trojan counsellor and friend of Hector who urged caution the night before the Greeks broke out.

Lucas's Licoraeus from North America has not been matched to a modern species; the plate shows a large brown swallowtail with yellow bands, blue and red hindwing spots and long tails, close to the tiger swallowtails.
It may be a dark or aberrant tiger swallowtail; Lucas placed it beside Turnus, the tiger swallowtail, on the same plate.
Named for Lycoreus, a son of Apollo and founder of Lycoreia on Parnassus.

n82-2.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
facts: The state butterfly of five American states and one of the most familiar insects of eastern North America, where it glides over gardens and woodland edges from spring to autumn.
Females come in two colours: the yellow tiger shown here and a dark form that mimics the poisonous pipevine swallowtail, commoner where that species flies.
Lucas used Turnus, Linnaeus's name of 1771; Linnaeus had already described the same insect as Glaucus in 1758, and that name is used today.
Named for Turnus, king of the Rutuli and Aeneas's rival in the Aeneid. The species is now Papilio glaucus, the tiger swallowtail.

n84-1.name: Asian Swallowtail
facts: The common swallowtail of Japan, China and Korea, where it lays on citrus in gardens; its caterpillars, green with a mock face, are a familiar sight on lemon trees.
It has become a laboratory animal: Japanese researchers use it to study colour vision, which is among the richest known in insects, and the genetics of wing pattern.
Named by Linnaeus for Xuthus, a son of Hellen and ancestor of the Ionians.

n84-2.name: Spicebush Swallowtail
facts: A swallowtail of eastern North America whose caterpillar is famous for its false eyespots: it rests in a rolled leaf of spicebush or sassafras and looks like a small green snake.
The adult is another mimic of the poisonous pipevine swallowtail, dark with a wash of blue-green on the hindwing.
Lucas's specimen came from the north-eastern United States, which supplied Paris with insects through the port of New York.
Named by Linnaeus for Troilus, the young prince of Troy slain by Achilles.

n86-1.name: Black Swallowtail
facts: The parsley worm of American gardens: its caterpillars feed on carrot, parsley, dill and fennel, and gardeners know the green and black banded larvae better than the adult.
It is the state butterfly of Oklahoma and New Jersey, and the female mimics the poisonous pipevine swallowtail.
Lucas's Asterias is the name Fabricius gave the dark form; Linnaeus had named the species Polyxenes in 1775.

Lucas, 1835: “This species of middling size is brownish black, with a yellow transverse band made up of triangular spots on the forewings and divided by black veins on the hindwings. The hind edge of the forewings is slightly toothed and preceded by a row of yellow dots; the hindwings have curved blunt teeth, a black tail of moderate length, and a tawny anal angle marked with a very black dot beneath a lunule of blue atoms.”
Asterias means starry; Fabricius's name for the black swallowtail, whose rows of yellow spots the engraver has picked out here.

n86-2.name: Cream-lined Swallowtail
facts: Godart named this swallowtail for Delalande, the Paris museum's collector at the Cape; Lucas's caption says California, which cannot be right, and the modern identity is the Madagascan cream-lined swallowtail, Papilio delalandei.
The figure shows a black swallowtail with cream bands and blue and red hindwing spots, with the tails clubbed at the tip.
Named for Pierre Antoine Delalande, the Paris museum's collector at the Cape of Good Hope, who died in 1823.
A kite swallowtail of South America with the longest tails in the family, white with black stripes and a red spot at the anal angle; it drinks in numbers at wet sand along Amazonian rivers.
Linnaeus named it in 1758 for Protesilaus, the first Greek to die at Troy, and it now gives its name to a whole genus of kite swallowtails.
Named by Linnaeus for Protesilaus, the first Greek to leap ashore at Troy and the first to die there.
Fabricius's Agapenor is an African swordtail with pale green bands; Lucas's caption gives Africa without more, and the modern identity has not been settled with confidence.
Agapenor led the Arcadians at Troy; the name sits among the Greek heroes Linnaeus and his followers gave to the swallowtails.
Named for Agapenor, leader of the Arcadians at Troy, whose ships were blown to Cyprus on the way home.

n98-1.name: Five-bar Swordtail
facts: A swordtail of India and South-east Asia, white with black bars across the forewing and long slender tails; it is a fast, low flier that settles to drink at wet earth and bird droppings.
Lucas called it Pompilius and cited Cramer's Antiphates as a synonym; Antiphates, Cramer's older name, is the one in use, and Lucas's Java is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white above with a very faint greenish tint, gently strengthened at the base and apex of the forewings; along the costa run seven transverse black bands, the three foremost nearly equal, the next two short, the two hindmost longer and broader, ending in a point and meeting near the inner angle. The hindwings have their lower edge cut by black lunules, mostly on an ashen ground.”
Named for Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome and founder of its religious calendar.

n98-2.name: Small Striped Swordtail
facts: A swordtail of the African savannas and forest edges, pale green-striped with long tails; Lucas's caption gives North America, which is a mistake, and his own synonym from Cramer, Policenes, gives the right identity.
The caterpillars feed on the custard-apple family, Annonaceae, as do most swordtails.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above, with an interrupted band, four transverse streaks and a row of marginal spots of pale green. The band curves inward and crosses the middle of all four wings; the streak nearest the body continues on the hindwings to above the anal angle, where it ends in a dot of carmine red.”
Named for Polyxena, Priam's daughter, sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles.

n100-1.name: Lesser Zebra
facts: A swallowtail that has abandoned the family look: it copies the striped tigers and glasswings of the Danainae so well in colour and slow flight that in the field it is easily passed over as one of them.
It flies in the forests of the Himalayan foothills, Burma, Malaya and the Indonesian islands; Lucas's Java is right.
Named for Macareus, a name borne by several figures of Greek myth, among them a son of Aeolus.

n100-2.name: Common Mime
facts: A swallowtail with two costumes: one form copies the black crows, Euploea, the other, shown here, copies the blue tiger, Tirumala, both of them poisonous.
Linnaeus described the two forms as separate species, Clytia and Dissimilis, in 1758; Lucas kept Dissimilis for this one, and it is now known to be the same insect.
It flies from India through China to the Philippines, and its caterpillars feed on trees of the laurel family.
Dissimilis means unlike in Latin: Linnaeus named the mime for looking nothing like its relatives.

n102-1.name: Volta Swallowtail
facts: A large swallowtail of the West and Central African rainforest, brown-black with a broad cream band; the female is the larger and paler.
Fabricius described it in 1775 from Sierra Leone as Zenobia, after the queen of Palmyra; Lucas's Zenobius is a masculine slip.

Lucas, 1835: “This is a large species; all its wings are slightly toothed, brownish black above, and crossed in the middle by a fairly broad white band faintly tinged with yellow, a little fringed on the hindwings and cut by fine black veins. The small notches of the forewings are edged with faintly yellowish dots, those of the hindwings with oblong spots of the same colour.”
Named for Zenobia, the third-century queen of Palmyra who defied Rome.

n102-2.name: Mimetic Swallowtail
facts: So closely does this African swallowtail copy the unpalatable Amauris butterflies in its cream-banded brown pattern and slow flight that it is simply called the mimetic swallowtail.
Lucas's Cafrerie is the old French name for the country of the Xhosa beyond the Cape frontier; the species in fact flies in the forests of West and Central Africa.

Lucas, 1835: “This species closely resembles Zenobius, but is much smaller and much less dark in colour. All the wings are toothed and finely edged with white on both surfaces; the forewings are reddish brown, crossed in the middle by a broad band finely cut by reddish veins and strongly interrupted towards the front.”
Named for Cynortas, a mythical king of Sparta.

n112-1.name: Blue Albatross
facts: An albatross, Appias, from New Guinea and the Aru Islands: the males are washed with pale blue, the females brown and white, and both are among the fastest fliers in the white family.
The frosted blue of Lucas's figure is the male; the scales carry a faint iridescence that the colourist could only hint at.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are nearly round, entire, of a frosted blue; the forewings have a black border, broadest at the apex and toothed inwardly near the base, and are lightly speckled with black, as are the veins. Beneath, the forewings are pearl grey, faintly yellow at the base, and near the base the hindwings carry silky, faintly bluish hairs.”
Celestina means heavenly, for the frosted blue of the wings.

n112-2.name: Common Melwhite
facts: A white of the American tropics from Mexico to Argentina, common along forest edges and one of the species that streams past in numbers during dry-season migrations.
Lucas's figure shows the black-tipped male; the female is heavily marked with yellow beneath.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings above, and the forewings beneath, are white, both surfaces ending in a fairly broad black border, curved on the hindwings and forming on the forewings a long triangle whose point reaches the inner angle. Beneath, the costa of the forewings is edged with black and washed with a yellow that fades from the border towards the base.”
Named for Licymnius, the uncle of Heracles.
Lucas's Thyria, from Java, has not been matched to a modern species with confidence; the plate shows an all-orange white with dark veins, which suggests a female of one of the Javan Appias or Delias.
Godart described a Pieris Thyria in 1819 from the Paris collection.
Named for Thyria, a town of Elis in Greece.

n114-1.name: Orange Albatross
facts: From New Guinea and New Britain; Lucas's Port Praslin is the French name for a harbour on New Ireland visited by the Bougainville and d'Entrecasteaux expeditions.
The underside of the hindwing is orange and shows through the white above, as Lucas noticed in his description.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are bluish white above, with the hind margin, the vein tips and the costa of the forewings black. The black band, broadest at the apex, is lightly toothed inwardly; the middle of the hindwings is white and faintly orange where the marigold-coloured patch beneath shows through.”
Named for Ada, the Carian queen who adopted Alexander the Great as her son.
Godart's Limnoria, from Brazil, is a white with black tips and a yellow hindwing; its modern identity has not been settled with confidence.
Limnoreia was one of the Nereids.
Named for Limnoreia, a Nereid.

n114-3.name: Western Dotted Border
facts: A West African white whose caterpillars feed on mistletoes high in the trees; the adults are slow fliers that birds avoid, and the row of dots along the wing edge gives the English name.
Cramer named it Poppaea, after Nero's empress, in the 1770s.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are white. The forewings carry at the apex an arched and widened patch, sometimes elliptical, sometimes joined into a continuous band, and their base is orange with a blackish costa. Beneath, the apex is paler and faintly greenish, the base a deeper orange spreading much further than above.”
Named for Poppaea Sabina, the wife of Nero.
Godart's Phaloe, from Brazil, has not been matched confidently; the plate shows a white with dark veins and a dark bar across the hindwing, in the manner of the Neotropical Itaballia and Perrhybris.
Phaloe was a Naiad.
Named for Phaloe, a Naiad.

n116-2.name: Lesser Albatross
facts: A white of India, South-east Asia and northern Australia that flies fast along forest streams and gathers on wet sand; Lucas's Coromandel and Java both lie within its range.
Wet-season and dry-season broods differ, the dry-season insects being smaller and less marked.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white faintly tinged with blue above, with a dark base. The forewings have the whole costa black and, at the tip, a border of the same colour, sinuous inwardly and widened at the apex, where it is divided by a broken band or by two white spots. Beneath, the hindwings are entirely pearl grey with a faint violet gleam.”
Named for Paulina, a Roman matron's name; Cramer and Fabricius favoured such names for the tropical whites.

n116-3.name: Calypso Caper White
facts: A caper white of the West African forest belt; Lucas's Côte d'Angole is the Angolan coast, at the southern end of its range.
Drury named it Calypso in 1773 after the nymph who detained Odysseus; the caterpillars, like those of all caper whites, feed on Capparis.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white above with a dark base. The male has at the tip of the forewings a black border, sinuous inwardly and broader at the apex, where it shows a transverse row of five or six white triangular spots pointing outward; the hindwings are edged by a run of closely set oval black spots.”
Named for Calypso, the nymph who kept Odysseus on her island for seven years.

n118-1.name: Caper White
facts: Famous in Australia for its mass migrations: in some spring seasons millions pour through Sydney and Brisbane over several days, moving from inland breeding grounds where their caper bushes have been stripped.
Fabricius named it Teutonia in 1775 and Sparrman named it Java a few years earlier; Java stands, and Lucas's Timor is within its range.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white above, with a broad black hind border entirely divided by a row of white spots, the foremost oval, the rest round and smaller. The forewings also have, towards the middle of the costa, a curved transverse black band, broader in the female than in the male; beneath, the hindwings are strongly veined with black and marked with deep yellow.”
Named for the Teutons; Fabricius often reached for tribal and place names when the classical stock ran thin.

n118-2.name: Zebra White
facts: An African white of dry savanna from Senegal to South Africa, barred with black above and beneath; Lucas left the locality blank on the caption.
The caterpillars feed on Boscia and Maerua, shrubs of the caper family.
Named for Eriphia, one of the nymphs who nursed the infant Dionysus.

n118-3.range: Lucas's specimen: Java, Bornéo, Indes Or.
facts: Lucas's Coronea, from Java, Borneo and the East Indies, awaits a confident identification; the figure shows an orange-and-black white with a pale border, perhaps a female of one of the Jezebels or albatrosses.
Fabricius described Papilio Coronea in 1793; Lucas also cites Donovan's Dejapea.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above in the male and yellow-tinged white in the female, with a black hind border sinuous on its inner side, very broad in the female. Both sexes are black beneath, with a very large orange patch at the base of the forewings and a transverse row of four or five oval greenish spots on the hind margin.”
Named for Coronea, the town of Boeotia where the Spartans fought in 394 BC.
Godart's Pitys, from Java, is a yellow white with a brown border; its modern identity has not been fixed, though it is probably a female of one of the Javan albatrosses, Appias.
Pitys was the nymph turned into a pine tree.
Named for Pitys, the nymph pursued by Pan and turned into a pine tree.
Fabricius's Judith, from Java, is a jezebel with yellow hindwings and a black-tipped white forewing; the plate suggests Delias, though the exact species is not settled.
The name is the biblical Judith who beheaded Holofernes.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are white above, with the base and most of the costa ashen, the veins black and the middle one much widened, and at the tip a black border carrying four or five small oblong white spots. The hindwings above are a fine yellow, turning orange towards the anal angle, with the whole hind margin black.”
Named for Judith, the biblical heroine who beheaded the Assyrian general Holofernes.

n128-3.name: Belisama Jezebel
facts: A jezebel of Java, Sumatra and the Lesser Sundas; like all Delias its underside is brighter than the upperside, a warning to birds that the caterpillars fed on mistletoe and made it distasteful.
Lucas's Amboine is probably an error; the species does not reach the Moluccas.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is white above, with the hind margin of the hindwings and two thirds of the costa of the forewings black, the forewings also bearing at the tip a very large triangular black space. Beneath, the forewings are black with a whitish crescent in the middle; the hindwings are ochre yellow, with a fairly broad black border saw-toothed on its inner side.”
Named for Belisama, a Celtic goddess equated by the Romans with Minerva.

Lucas's Philyra, from Amboina, is a jezebel-like white with orange and black; his own text cites Linnaeus's Hyparete as a synonym, so it is close to or the same as the Painted Jezebel on the next plate.
Philyra was the mother of the centaur Chiron.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is bluish white above, with a black apex divided transversely by an arched band of four or five oval white spots, and a narrow black border to the hindwings. The female is dull white above with each wing broadly edged in black; both sexes are black beneath, with about the front third of all four wings yellow and pricked with blackish.”
Named for Philyra, the Oceanid who was mother of the centaur Chiron.

n130-2.name: Isse Jezebel
facts: A jezebel from Amboina and the neighbouring Moluccan islands, described by Cramer in the 1770s from specimens brought home by the Dutch East India Company.
The yellow underside with black-ringed spots is the warning colour typical of the group.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are white above with a black apex divided transversely by an arched band of four or five white spots; the hindwings are faintly bluish above with a fairly broad black border cut by a run of whitish dots. Beneath, the hindwings are clouded yellow from base to middle, then black to the tip, with a marginal row of six marigold-coloured spots, three heart-shaped and three nearly round.”
Named for Isse, daughter of Macareus, loved by Apollo in the guise of a shepherd.

n130-3.name: Common Jezebel
facts: One of the best-known butterflies of India and Sri Lanka, sailing slowly among the treetops and showing its brilliant yellow, red and black underside to warn birds off.
The caterpillars feed on mistletoes on mango and other trees, and the adult is often the first butterfly a visitor to India learns to name.

Lucas, 1835: “Above, the male is bluish white with black veins, more pronounced on the forewings than the hindwings, and each wing ends in a broad black border faintly fringed with whitish, arched and gently sinuous inwardly. Along its whole length this border is divided by a row of fairly large oval spots, white on the forewings and faintly flesh-coloured on the hindwings.”
Named for Epicharis, the freedwoman who kept silent under torture during the conspiracy against Nero.

n132-1.name: Painted Jezebel
facts: A jezebel of South-east Asia from India to the Philippines whose underside is painted red, yellow and black, colours the engraver has shown through the white upperside.
Linnaeus described it in 1758 as Hyparete, after the wife of Alcibiades; Lucas's Java and China both hold it.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is a slightly bluish white above, with the hind margin of the hindwings black. The forewings end in a black band forming a long triangle, its inner side sinuous, cut along its length by a run of six whitish spots, the first five elliptical and larger, the sixth rounded. All four wings are entirely veined with black beneath.”
Named for Hipparete, the wife of the Athenian statesman Alcibiades.

n132-2.name: Black Jezebel
facts: A jezebel of eastern Australia from Queensland to Victoria, black above with red at the base of the hindwing beneath; the caterpillars feed in groups on mistletoe.
Fabricius named it Nigrina in 1775; Lucas's New Holland is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above, especially in the male. The forewings have the costa lightly edged with black and, at the tip, a large deep black triangular space, arched and faintly sinuous inwardly, divided opposite the apex by a transverse line of three or four small white spots. Both sexes are brownish black beneath, dusted with white, with a deep yellow oblique band at the apex of the forewings.”
Nigrina means blackish in Latin.

n132-3.name: Imperial Jezebel
facts: The largest jezebel of south-eastern Australia, whose caterpillars feed on mistletoes hanging in eucalyptus trees; the adults gather at the mistletoe flowers in autumn.
Donovan named it Harpalyce, after a Thracian warrior maiden, in his Insects of New Holland of 1805.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above, broadly edged with black at their tips. The forewings carry at the apex an arched, spotted white band; the hindwings are unspotted. Beneath, both are velvet black with a whitish lunule in the middle, and the hindwings are crossed by a vermilion red band, spotted and winding, from the front edge to the inner edge.”
Named for Harpalyce, the Thracian huntress raised by her father to fight as a warrior.

n134-1.name: Spotted Jezebel
facts: Known in Australia as the wood white, it ranges across the south of the continent and is one of the commonest jezebels near Sydney and Adelaide; its caterpillars feed on mistletoe and on native cherry.
The red and yellow spots of the underside show faintly through the white in Lucas's figure.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are bluish white above with a very broad black hind border on which are ranged round spots close to the ground colour. Below the costa of the forewings, near this border, the male has a black space divided across by a white lunule; in the female this space merges with the border and shows, besides the lunule, an angular white band facing the apex.”
Named for Aganippe, the spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses.

n134-2.name: Chiapas White
facts: Perrhybris pyrrha is a white of the American tropics whose female wears a tiger's coat: orange, yellow and black stripes that copy the poisonous tiger butterflies, while the male stays white.
The insect on Lucas's plate is the striped female, which is why it looks nothing like a white.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are white, with a light black border at the tip of the hindwings and along the costa of the forewings, which carry at the apex a triangular black space whose point rests on the middle of the hind edge. Beneath, the hindwings are brownish black with two transverse bands, the front one pale sulphur yellow, the hind one white washed with yellow, separated by a streak of marigold red.”
Named for Pyrrha, wife of Deucalion, who with him repeopled the earth after the flood by throwing stones over their shoulders.

n134-3.name: Large Vagrant
facts: A big white of the African forests from Guinea to Uganda, whose females come in several colours; the greenish white of the figure is one of them.
Vagrants, Nepheronia, are strong fliers that patrol forest edges and are hard to catch, which is why old collections hold few of them.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings above are white faintly tinged with green. The forewings are edged at the tip by a very black band of moderate width forming a long triangle pointing downward, its inner side sinuous and cut by five or six small longitudinal black strokes; the hindwings are unspotted. Beneath, the black of the costa and tip is replaced by pale ochre yellow.”
Named for Argia, daughter of Adrastus and wife of Polynices in the tale of Thebes.

n144-1.name: West Virginia White
facts: A spring white of the eastern American woods that flies for a few weeks while the toothworts its caterpillars eat are in leaf; it is now threatened by garlic mustard, an invasive plant that tempts the females to lay but poisons the young.
Lucas left the locality blank; the species was named for Virginia by Edwards in 1870, so the name on the plate is an older one that happens to coincide.
Named for Virginia, the colony, or for the Roman maiden of that name; the species is American.

n144-2.name: Common Wanderer
facts: A white of India and South-east Asia whose male is veined with pale blue and whose female copies the blue tiger butterfly so closely that it is often mistaken for one.
It flies high and fast in the forest canopy and comes down to drink at wet ground; Lucas's Java is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is greenish white above with the veins and the hind margin black; the costa of the forewings is likewise black, and their tip shows a marginal row of whitish dots. In the female these dots appear on all four wings, the ground is less green and the veins are wider. Beneath, the hindwings are pearl grey with a faint violet gleam.”
Named for the Valerii, one of the great patrician families of Rome.
Godart's Endeis, from Brazil, has not been identified with confidence; the plate shows a white with black forewing tips and a yellow flush at the base of the hindwing.
Endeis was the grandmother of Achilles.
Named for Endeis, mother of Peleus and grandmother of Achilles.

n146-1.name: Psyche
facts: The smallest white of Asia, a wisp of a butterfly that flutters weakly a few inches above the grass in shady places from India to the Philippines and Australia.
Fabricius named it Nina in 1793; the single black spot on each forewing is its only mark.
Nina is a girl's name, not a myth; Fabricius gave it to this little white in 1793.

n146-2.name: Amboina Orange-tip
facts: The orange giant of the Moluccas, one of the largest whites in the world; the whole upper surface is orange rather than the white with orange tips of its relatives.
Cramer described it from Amboina in the 1770s; Lucas's Java is doubtful, since the species is confined to the Moluccas.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are a cheerful tawny above, with the veins black and widened; the hind margin is also black, with two rows of unequal white dots preceded outwardly by a small broken edging of the same colour. The forewings have at the apex a large triangular black space crossed obliquely by a fine white angular band made up of five touching spots.”
Named for Leucippe, a name of several heroines meaning white horse.

n146-3.name: Great Orange-tip
facts: The largest white in Asia, with a wingspan that can reach a hand's breadth; the male's orange tips flash in flight and vanish when it settles, because the underside is mottled like a dead leaf.
It flies from India to Japan and the Philippines, drinks at wet sand, and its caterpillars feed on capers; Lucas's Java is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings above are a vivid tawny, lightly glazed with red, with a clouded greenish-yellow base and the veins and whole outer edge black; parallel to the hind edge runs a row of black triangular spots pointing towards the base, larger and closer in the female. The hindwings are a fine lemon yellow above, edged in the female by a black band toothed inwardly.”
Glaucippe means grey-green horse in Greek, a companion name to Leucippe given by Linnaeus in 1758.

n148-1.name: White Orange-tip
facts: An orange-tip of the dry plains of India and Sri Lanka, white with an orange patch enclosed in black; it flies low over scrub in the hot months.
Lucas's Bengal and Coromandel are both within its Indian range.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is bluish white above, the female yellowish white. In both sexes the forewings carry at the tip a very large triangular black space bearing a broad, arched patch of dawn orange, a little paler in the female and cut by a transverse line of black dots. The hindwings have the hind margin black in both sexes and the edge slightly sinuous.”
Named for Marianne; Cramer used the names of women of his own day as freely as those of antiquity.

n148-2.name: Yellow Orange-tip
facts: The commonest orange-tip of India and South-east Asia, yellow in the wet season and paler and smaller in the dry; the caterpillars feed on Capparis.
Linnaeus named it Pyrene in 1764 after the Corinthian spring; Lucas's China, Bengal and Coromandel are all correct.

Lucas, 1835: “Both sexes are lemon yellow above. The forewings have at the tip a very large triangular black space on which sits an arched patch of dawn orange, narrowed at its lower end and a little paler in the female; the hindwings have a black hind margin. Beneath, all four wings are greenish yellow with usually only a very small blackish dot in the middle of each.”
Named for Pirene, the fountain of Corinth where Pegasus was said to drink.
Fabricius's Oenippe, from China, Bengal and Java, is a lemon-yellow orange-tip with a black border; the plate suggests one of the Ixias, but the species has not been fixed with confidence.
Lucas notes the transverse band is yellow or pale orange according to sex, and the underside carries a row of eye-like brownish spots.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are lemon yellow above, with the margin of the hindwings and the rear half of the forewings black. The forewings also carry, opposite the apex, an oblique transverse band, yellow or pale dawn according to sex, sinuous on both sides and marked with a dot near its lower end. This species is found in China, in Bengal and in the island of Java.”
Named for Oenippe; Fabricius's coinage from the Greek for wine-horse.
Ixias venilia is an orange-tip of Java and the Lesser Sunda Islands, yellow with an orange-and-black apex, described by Godart in 1819.
Venilia was a Roman sea nymph; Lucas's Java is right.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings above are faintly ashen at the base, lemon yellow along the inner edge and black over the rest, with a very large patch of dawn orange rounded outwardly, marked with a black dot in its middle and divided by veins of that colour. The hindwings are lemon yellow above with a black border, sometimes very narrow, sometimes fairly broad, toothed on its inner side.”
Named for Venilia, a Roman sea nymph, wife of Janus in some accounts.

n150-2.name: Large Salmon Arab
facts: An Arab, Colotis, of the desert edges from Syria and Arabia to India; its caterpillars feed on the toothbrush tree, Salvadora, and the adult is salmon pink rather than white.
Olivier collected the type on his journey through the Ottoman empire in the 1790s, which is why Lucas gives Syria.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are pale tawny above with a row of black dots along the hind edge. The forewings have a black dot in the middle and, between this and the marginal dots, a curved, broken transverse black streak that does not reach the inner edge. Beneath, the hindwings are very pale yellow with a faintly blackish waved streak continuing the streak of the forewings.”
Fausta means fortunate in Latin, and was the name of Constantine's empress.

n150-3.name: Three-spot Crimson-tip
facts: A crimson-tip of the Sudanese savanna, from Senegal to Ethiopia; Lucas's Nubie, the Nile valley south of Egypt, is exactly where the Paris museum was receiving insects from in the 1830s.
The red tips carry three black spots, hence the English name.
Eupompe means fair procession in Greek, the name of a Nereid.

n150-4.name: Crimson-tip
facts: A butterfly of dry scrub from Africa to India whose forewing tips are dipped in crimson; it flies low and fast in the heat of the day and rests with wings closed on bare ground.
Fabricius named it Danae in 1775, after the mother of Perseus; Lucas's East Indies is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are white above. The forewings have at the tip a triangular black space almost entirely filled by a patch of fine carmine red; the hindwings carry a run of black triangular spots along the hind edge. Beneath, the apex of the forewings is whitish with a narrow reddish band cut lengthwise by a line of black dots.”
Named for Danaë, mother of Perseus, to whom Zeus came as a shower of gold.

n160-1.name: Round-winged Orange-tip
facts: An African orange-tip of savanna and coastal bush from Senegal to Angola and across to Kenya; Lucas's Angolan coast is within its range.
Linnaeus named it Evippe in 1758; the orange tips vary from deep to pale between seasons and regions.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are white above with a faintly dark base. The forewings have at the apex a fairly large triangular black space bearing a patch of vivid tawny, rounded outwardly, sinuous inwardly and a little narrowed at its lower end, and a very small black dot in the middle. The hindwings carry on the hind margin a row of nearly round black spots.”
Named for Euippe, one of the Danaids.
Cramer's Achine, of unknown locality on Lucas's caption, is a white with a pale tawny apex and black border; it is probably an African Colotis, but the species has not been fixed.
The name is Cramer's and its origin is obscure.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are white faintly tinged with yellow above, with a black base. The forewings have the apex black with a pale tawny patch rounded outwardly and deeply cleft, and a black dot in the middle, more or less distinct. The hindwings are broadly edged with black at the tip, with a broken row of fairly large white dots.”
Named for Achine; Cramer's spelling of a name of uncertain origin.
Colotis evarne is an African orange-tip of dry country from the Sahel to East Africa; Lucas could give no locality.
Klug described it in 1829 from Ehrenberg's collections in Nubia and Arabia, only six years before this plate.
Named for Evarne, one of the Nereids.

n160-4.name: Purple-tip
facts: The male has forewing tips of iridescent purple, unique among the orange-tips and shown on Lucas's plate; the female's tips are black or orange.
It flies in the savannas of eastern and southern Africa, where the caterpillars feed on capers.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are white, the base speckled with blackish. The forewings have at the tip an arched black border, narrow towards the inner angle and broad opposite the apex, where it is divided obliquely by a fine and very brilliant violet band, rounded outwardly; in the middle is a very black dot that repeats on the underside.”
Named for Ione, a sea nymph, one of the Nereids.

n162-1.name: Tailed Orange
facts: A yellow of Central America and the Caribbean whose dry-season form grows a short tail on the hindwing, which the wet-season form lacks.
Lucas's Jamaica is correct; Fabricius named it Proterpia in 1775.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are canary yellow with a black border fringed with whitish outwardly, faintly sinuous inwardly and ending in a point at the inner angle; in the male the costa is also broadly edged with black, and from the base runs a straight black line along almost the whole lower edge, which is orange. The hindwings are white above with a black border finely and irregularly toothed towards the base.”
Named for Proterpia; Fabricius's coinage from the Greek for delighting first.

n162-2.name: Common Grass Yellow
facts: Probably the most abundant butterfly across Asia, Africa and Australia, a small yellow that flutters over lawns and roadsides everywhere from Japan to Cape Town.
Linnaeus named it Hecabe in 1758 after the queen of Troy; the black border shrinks in the dry season and widens in the wet.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of all four wings is a fine yellow. The forewings have at the tip a black border lightly edged with yellow outwardly and very sinuous inwardly, beginning in a point towards the middle of the costa and ending at the inner angle in a very broad hook; the hindwings have a narrower black border, arched and crenellated only on the side facing the base.”
Named for Hecuba, queen of Troy and mother of Hector. Linnaeus gave the name in 1758 to this common yellow of the East.
Eurema candida is a grass yellow of the Moluccas and New Guinea, deep yellow with a broad black border; Cramer described it from Amboina, as Lucas's caption says.
Candida means shining white, and refers to the pale underside.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a fine deep yellow above, with a broad black border embracing their outline, a little narrower on the costa of the hindwings. Beneath, the border is a less deep black; the antennae are black, the body blackish above and yellow beneath, with a blackish line along the sides reaching the anal part. Found in the island of Amboina.”
Candida means shining white in Latin, a curious name for a yellow butterfly; it refers to the white of the underside.

n162-4.name: Sleepy Orange
facts: A yellow of the southern United States and Mexico, orange with a black border; the small dash on the forewing looks like a closed eye, which gave it the name sleepy.
The caterpillars feed on Senna, and the adults stream north in late summer as far as the Great Lakes; Lucas's Virginia is within its range.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a vivid tawny above with a fairly broad black border, sinuous below, narrowed in the middle on the forewings and widened on the hindwings. The forewings also carry a black crescent in the middle. Beneath, the wings are paler and the border is replaced by blackish atoms; the hindwings are yellow with several rust-coloured spots.”
Named for Nicippe, a daughter of Pelops.

n164-1.name: Banded Yellow
facts: A yellow of the American tropics from Mexico to Argentina; the male carries a black bar along the inner edge of the forewing, which Lucas described and the engraver drew.
Cramer described it in the 1770s, and Lucas's Brazil is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above, with a broad transverse band of blood red across the disc, cleft at each end and not reaching the tip of the hindwings. On the forewings this band is preceded outwardly by a narrower white band of five touching spots, and near the hind edge of each wing runs a line of white dots.”
Named for Elatea, an ancient town of Phocis in central Greece.

n164-2.name: Small Grass Yellow
facts: An Australian grass yellow of the tropical north and the inland, small and pale; Lucas's East Indies is a slip, since Donovan described it from New Holland.
The name Smilax is the nymph who loved Crocus and became the bindweed.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is a fine yellow above, the female a pale sulphur yellow, with a brownish-black border edged with reddish outwardly and sinuous inwardly, very narrow on the hindwings of the male and formed, on those of the female, by a run of spots of which the foremost is much the largest. Beneath, the forewings are yellow with a black dot in the middle.”
Named for Smilax, the nymph who loved the youth Crocus and was turned into the bindweed that bears her name.

n164-3.name: Small Salmon Arab
facts: An Arab of the dry plains from Africa to India, salmon pink above with a fine dark border; Lucas's Coromandel coast is a classic locality for it.
The caterpillars feed on the toothbrush tree, Salvadora, in saline and desert ground.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of the wings is a shining silvery green, ending on the forewings in a large triangular space of dark green and on the hindwings in a clouded band carrying a row of black dots. Beneath, all four wings are meadow green with a few rusty spots in the middle and light silvery shades along the inner edge. Found on the west coast of Africa.”
Named for Amata, queen of the Latins and mother of Lavinia in the Aeneid.

n164-4.name: Clouded Sulphur
facts: The common yellow of North American fields and roadsides, whose caterpillars feed on clover and alfalfa; it is so abundant over lucerne fields that farmers call it the alfalfa butterfly.
It hybridises with the orange sulphur, Colias eurytheme, wherever the two meet; Lucas's northern America is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are canary yellow above, with a fairly broad black border divided, on the forewings of the female, by a strongly interrupted yellow spotted band. The forewings have an oblong black dot towards the middle of the costa; the hindwings have a pale, rounded orange patch on the disc, and beneath two silver dots, the outer one smaller.”
Named for Philodice, a Naiad, wife of Leucippus.

n164-5.name: Southern Dogface
facts: The black on the forewing outlines the head of a poodle, eye and all, which gives the butterfly its name; it flies in the southern United States and south to Argentina.
Stoll named it Caesonia, after Caligula's wife, in 1790.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are a fine yellow above. The forewings, whose apex is a little sharp, have the front half of the costa dark, a fairly large black dot in the middle, and at the tip a very broad black border whose inner side is sinuous and deeply notched in the middle, its outer side finely cut with yellow and red-brown. The hindwings are rounded and marked in the middle with two orange dots.”
Named for Caesonia, the last wife of the emperor Caligula.

n174-1.name: Orange Migrant
facts: A migrant, Catopsilia, of South-east Asia and Australia, orange and cream; it flies fast and straight and undertakes long seasonal movements, and its caterpillars feed on Cassia and Senna.
Linnaeus named it Scylla in 1763; Lucas's China, Bengal and Java are all within its range.
Named for Scylla, the sea monster of the Strait of Messina in the Odyssey.
Godart's Evadne, locality unknown on the caption, is a greenish-white sulphur with lemon-yellow at the base; Lucas cites Cramer's Alcmeone, and the figure resembles the female of a Phoebis.
Evadne threw herself on her husband's pyre at Thebes.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a shining greenish white; the forewings are lightly edged with black, and the lemon yellow of the upperside reaches the middle of the forewings and the margin of the hindwings. All four wings are greenish beneath; the body is greenish white, the antennae black with a whitish club.”
Named for Evadne, who threw herself on her husband Capaneus's funeral pyre at Thebes.

n174-3.name: Apricot Sulphur
facts: An apricot-coloured sulphur of the American tropics from Mexico to Brazil, common in gardens and along rivers; the caterpillars feed on Cassia and Inga.
Fabricius named it Argante in 1775; Lucas's Guiana and Brazil are correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are an orange yellow, a little shot with colour, above. Beneath, they are a deep ochre yellow, with silvery discal dots and winding reddish lines accompanied by a multitude of rusty atoms; in some individuals the silver dots have little brilliance. This species is found in Guiana and Brazil.”
Named for Argante, an Amazon queen in Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered.

n176-1.name: Straight-line Sulphur
facts: A lemon-yellow sulphur of the American tropics named for the straight brown line across the underside of both wings, which Lucas described.
Linnaeus described it in 1758; it is a migrant that occasionally reaches Texas.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of all four wings is a fine lemon yellow, a little matt towards the tip. Beneath, they are greenish or greyish and shining, with a rusty line running from the apex of the forewings towards the middle of the inner edge of the hindwings. The body is lemon yellow above and faintly yellowish white beneath.”
Named by Linnaeus in 1758 for Trite, a name of Athena.

n176-2.name: Orange-barred Sulphur
facts: A large sulphur of the American tropics that reaches Florida; the male has an orange bar across the forewing and an orange flush on the hindwing, both visible in Lucas's figure.
The caterpillars feed on Senna and Cassia and are patterned yellow and black to match the flowers.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are a vivid lemon yellow, a little matt towards the tip, and almost rounded in shape. The forewings have towards the middle a transverse orange patch of varying size; the hindwings are orange, sometimes from the middle to the tip, sometimes only at the tip, and the hind edge of both is cut by very small black dots.”
Philea means loving in Greek; Linnaeus's name for this orange-barred sulphur.
Godart's Leachiana, from Brazil, is a large greenish-white sulphur with an orange forewing patch; the plate resembles the Anteos angled-sulphurs, but the identity is not settled.
Godart named it for William Elford Leach of the British Museum.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are entire and greenish white. The upperside of the forewings shows at the slightly pointed apex a fine triangular patch of dawn orange running from the middle of the costa to the middle of the hind edge, bordered outwardly by a black line and marked on its inner side by a large black dot. Beneath, all the wings are greenish white with a rusty, faintly purplish patch near the centre.”
Named for William Elford Leach, zoologist at the British Museum, who died in 1836, the year this book was completed.

n178-2.name: White Angled-Sulphur
facts: A large sulphur with angular wings that looks like a leaf when settled; the yellow patch on the forewing and the red-ringed spots beneath are its only marks.
It is a strong flier of the American tropics that strays north to Texas and Kansas; Godart named it Clorinde, after Tasso's warrior maiden, in 1824.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are greenish white above with a central orange dot having a black pupil. The forewings also carry, towards the middle of the costa, a large patch of lemon yellow. Beneath, the wings are greenish and faintly netted, with a flesh-coloured central dot answering the eye-spot of the opposite surface.”
Named for Clorinda, the warrior maiden of Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered, killed unknowingly by the knight who loved her.

n180-1.name: Gnidus Metalmark
facts: A metalmark of the Guianas and Amazon whose underside is studded with mirror-bright silver spots, which Lucas counted at about twenty on the hindwing; the long, fringed tails are part of the same wing.
Metalmarks, Riodinidae, are small tropical butterflies that often rest upside down beneath leaves, and many, like this one, are seldom seen except when they descend to flowers.

Lucas, 1835: “In the male the wings are white on both surfaces, with the base tawny and the tip black; the tip of the forewings shows above a run of small white strokes. Beneath, the hindwings carry towards the hind edge some twenty silver spots, the three at each end elongated on a white ground, the others round on a rusty ground, all edged with black.”
Named for Cnidus, the Greek city of Asia Minor famous for its statue of Aphrodite.

Linnaeus's Lysippus is a metalmark of the Guianas and Brazil, black with an orange band on each wing and a red spot at the anal angle; its exact modern placement among the riodinids has not been settled here.
The name honours Lysippus, sculptor to Alexander the Great.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with an orange band, more or less narrow. On the forewings the band descends obliquely from the middle of the costa to the inner angle, where it bends a little; on the hindwings it is arched outwardly and runs from the apex to the anal angle, near which is an oblong red dot. Beneath, the space between base and band shows a multitude of small pale ochre dots.”
Named for Lysippus, the sculptor of Alexander the Great.
Fabricius's Phareus is a small crimson metalmark of the Guianas and Brazil, red with black borders; Lucas put it in Erycina, and its modern genus has not been fixed here.
The name comes from Pharos, the lighthouse island of Alexandria.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a shining carmine red, with the outer margin and the costa of the forewings black. The black of the costa shows three unequal teeth above and reaches beyond the middle of the surface beneath; the hindwings often have a small black lunule at their centre. The body is red above and yellowish beneath.”
Named for Pharos, the island lighthouse of Alexandria.
A long-tailed hairstreak from Java of the group called imperials, whose white hindwing tails can be longer than the wing itself and twitch in the breeze to draw a bird's strike away from the head.
Godart named it Jafra, after the port of Jaffa, in 1824; Lucas's Java is right.
Named for Jaffa, the ancient port of Palestine.

n182-1.name: Cambridge Blue
facts: The largest hairstreak of the American tropics, a pale shimmering blue the colour of the Cambridge rowing crews, with two tails on each hindwing.
Linnaeus named it Marsyas in 1758, after the satyr flayed by Apollo; Lucas's Brazil is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a greenish violet blue, changing to violet, with the whole costa and the apex of the forewings black. Beneath, they are lilac or pale shining violet, with seven or eight black dots ringed with whitish scattered over the middle of each wing; the anal region of the hindwings is greenish blue with two short white bands. The tails are black tipped with white.”
Named for Marsyas, the satyr who challenged Apollo to a music contest and was flayed for losing.
Olynthus narbal is a hairstreak of the Guianas and Brazil, cornflower blue above and dark beneath with a red flash at the base of the wings, exactly as Lucas described.
Stoll named it in 1790 for Narbal, the Tyrian admiral of Fénelon's Télémaque, a novel every French schoolboy of the day had read.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are a shining cornflower blue above with a black apex; the forewings of the male have a greyish eye-spot towards the middle of the costa. Beneath, they are dark brown with the origin of the costa red on all four wings; the hindwings carry a white, waved, broken transverse line edged with black on its inner side, and two black eye-spots. Found in Guiana and Brazil.”
Named for Narbal, the Tyrian admiral in Fénelon's Télémaque, a favourite book of the eighteenth century.
Fabricius's Longinus, from Bengal, is a blue with a cornflower upperside and satin-grey underside; it belongs among the oakblues or hairstreaks of India, but the species has not been fixed.
Longinus was the Greek critic credited with the treatise On the Sublime.

Lucas, 1835: “In the male the wings are a shining cornflower blue above, in the female a pale violet blue, with the apex of the forewings and the outer edge of the hindwings brownish black. Both sexes are a whitish satin grey beneath with a waved line of small black arcs, and the hindwings have at the anal angle two black eyes with a tawny iris, separated by a cluster of silvery blue atoms. This species is found in Bengal.”
Named for Longinus, the Greek critic to whom the treatise On the Sublime is attributed.

n182-4.name: Centaur Oakblue
facts: An oakblue of India and South-east Asia whose caterpillars are tended by ants in return for a sugary secretion; the ants guard them, and the butterflies lay only where the right ants live.
The upper surface is a deep shot blue that vanishes when the wings close over a plain brown underside.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is a deep velvet violet above, with the channel of the hindwings blackish. Beneath, the wings are blackish brown netted with grey, with a run of three golden-green rings on the middle of the forewings and a small band of atoms of the same green at the anal angle of the hindwings, ending in a large black dot. The tail is black with a white tip.”
Named for Helos, a town of Laconia whose people became the helots of Sparta.
Euploea eunice is a crow of Java and the neighbouring islands, one of the black milkweed butterflies whose caterpillars feed on poisonous figs and oleander relatives and pass the poison on.
Males carry a brush of scent scales on the hindwing and court with a perfume made from alkaloids gathered at withered plants.
Named for Eunice, one of the Nereids.

n184-2.name: Blue-spotted Crow
facts: A crow of southern China and South-east Asia whose black wings flash violet-blue in the light and carry rows of white and blue spots; Lucas noted how the sheen shifts from violet to azure with the angle.
Linnaeus named it Midamus in 1758; the crows are poisonous milkweed butterflies that fly slowly and are copied by several harmless species.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are velvet black above, with a shot gleam from violet blue to azure according to the light; their front half is unspotted, the rest carries a great many white dots, the outer ones smaller and ranged along the edge. The hindwings above are brownish black, matt ash grey towards the apex; beneath, they show a dozen small violet spots between the middle and the apex.”
Named by Linnaeus for Midamus; the name is his own coinage.

n194-1.name: Friar
facts: A black and white milkweed butterfly of West African forests, poisonous and slow, and the model that one form of the mocker swallowtail's female copies exactly; the two hang on plates 13 and 46 of this book without Lucas knowing they were connected.
Linnaeus named it Niavius in 1758; Lucas's Guinea is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are black on both surfaces and crossed between the middle and the tip by a fairly broad white band, sinuous on its sides and cut by fine veins of the ground colour, preceded outwardly by one or two white dots and inwardly by four or five more. The hindwings above are brownish black with a white patch set transversely at the base.”
Named for Niavius; Linnaeus's coinage, of uncertain meaning.

n194-2.name: Common Tiger
facts: The striped tiger of India and South-east Asia, for two centuries confused with the American monarch, Danaus plexippus, to which Lucas's caption assigns it; his own synonym, Cramer's Genutia, gives the correct Asian species.
Like the monarch it is poisonous from milkweeds eaten as a caterpillar, flies slowly and is copied by harmless mimics, among them the female of the common wanderer on plate 33.
Lucas's East Indies is right for Genutia and wrong for the monarch, which did not reach Asia until it spread across the Pacific in the nineteenth century.
Named for Plexippus, uncle of Meleager, killed by him after the Calydonian boar hunt. The Monarch has carried the name since 1758.

Lucas's Hegesippe, from Sumatra, is a milkweed butterfly, orange and black with a white band at the forewing tip and white streaks on the hindwing; the species has not been fixed with confidence, though the pattern is that of the tigers, Danaus.
Cramer described a Papilio Hegesippus in the 1770s.

Lucas, 1835: “The ground of the forewings is black, and at the base is a large longitudinal tawny patch divided unequally in three by a forked black vein; opposite the apex is a white, spotted transverse band preceded outwardly by two marginal lines of white dots. The hindwings are brownish black with two rows of white dots on the hind margin and eight longitudinal white streaks running to the base.”
Named for Hegesippus, the Athenian orator and rival of Demosthenes' enemies.

n196-2.range: Lucas's specimen: Ile de Java, d'Amboine
facts: Lucas's Cleone, from Java and Amboina, is a green-striped milkweed butterfly of the tiger group; Cramer's Cleona, which Lucas cites, is one of the glassy tigers, Ideopsis or Parantica, but the species has not been fixed here.
The green of the figure would have been a yellowish white in life; the colourist has strengthened it.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above and dark brown beneath. The forewings carry on their front half three longitudinal spots of shining greenish yellow, two converging at the base and enclosing the third, which is much shorter; opposite the apex is a transparent transverse band faintly tinged with yellow, followed by white dots in two lines parallel to the hind edge.”
Named for Cleone, a nymph, daughter of the river Asopus.

n198-1.name: Paper Kite
facts: The rice-paper butterfly of the Moluccas and Philippines, one of the tree nymphs, whose great translucent wings carry it in a slow floating flight through the forest, seldom flapping; it is poisonous and unhurried because nothing eats it.
Linnaeus named it Idea in 1763; today it is one of the most popular butterflies in glasshouses because it lives long and flies gently among visitors.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are elliptical, entire and a little transparent. Their upperside is greyish white with black veins and a black hind border, fairly broad, very sinuous on its inner side and divided across its whole width, at least on the forewings, by a run of large white dots, some round, some oval; between each vein, towards the tip, is a black lance-shaped spot reaching the border.”
Named for Agelaus, a Greek name meaning leader of the people.

n200-1.name: Sara Longwing
facts: A longwing of the American tropics, black shot with blue and banded with yellow; it roosts in groups at night and the males wait on the pupae of females to mate the moment they emerge.
Like all Heliconius it feeds as a caterpillar on passion vines and as an adult on pollen, which it dissolves on its tongue and which gives it a life of several months, remarkable for a butterfly.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are deep black above with a blue gleam at the base. The forewings have two oblique transverse patches of sulphur yellow, one in the middle and one near the apex, the latter very narrow and made of four touching spots; the hindwings are unspotted above, their hind edge a little toothed and finely edged with white at the notches.”
Sara is a plain Hebrew name; Fabricius gave it to this small longwing in 1793.

n200-2.name: Postman
facts: The most studied butterfly in the tropics: across South America its races each match the local race of a second species, Heliconius erato, so closely that two poisonous butterflies share one warning livery, a case Fritz Müller explained in 1879.

Lucas placed the postman and its co-mimic Phyllis, which is a race of erato, on the same plate without knowing they were different species; the two were only separated with confidence in the twentieth century.
Adults gather pollen on their tongues, an ability unique to this group among butterflies, and live for months on the amino acids it supplies.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are a fairly deep black above. The forewings carry in the middle a broad transverse band of dull minium red, a little oblique, ending almost in a point below and more sinuous in the female than in the male; the hindwings are unspotted. Beneath, the hindwings are brownish black with the front half of the costa dull sulphur yellow and a few blood-red dots ranged in a half circle against the base.”
Named by Linnaeus for Melpomene, the Muse of tragedy.

n200-3.name: Red Postman
facts: Phyllis is the south-eastern Brazilian race of Heliconius erato, the partner in the most famous case of mutual mimicry in nature; its companion on this plate, Melpomene, is the other partner.
Erato and melpomene are told apart by the underside: erato has four red dots at the base of the hindwing where melpomene has three, a detail Lucas could not have known to look for.

Lucas, 1835: “Between the middle and the apex the forewings carry a broad transverse band of more or less vivid vermilion red starting from the costa, with a single tooth outwardly near its lower end and not reaching the inner edge; at the base is a longitudinal yellow line ending in a dot. The hindwings have near their origin a straight band of sulphur yellow of moderate width.”
Named for Phyllis, the Thracian princess who hanged herself waiting for Demophon and became an almond tree.

n202-1.name: Zebra Longwing
facts: The state butterfly of Florida, black with yellow zebra stripes; it roosts in groups of a dozen or more on the same twig night after night and returns to the same flowers on a daily round.
Males find female pupae by scent and sit on them, mating the instant the female emerges; the adults feed on pollen and live for months.
Linnaeus named it Charitonia in 1767 after the Graces; Lucas's America is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are black with bands of sulphur yellow. The forewings have three, the two outer ones transverse and oblique, the inner running straight from the base to the middle of the surface, where it bends a little to reach the hind edge; the hindwings have two transverse bands, the upper broad, straight and continuous, the lower curved and made of dots.”
Named by Linnaeus for the Charites, the Graces of Greek myth.

n202-2.name: Clearwing Mimic-Queen
facts: Not a longwing at all but a milkweed butterfly, Lycorea, that has taken on the tiger pattern of the poisonous ithomiines it flies with; Lucas placed it among the Heliconia on the strength of that pattern.
Its caterpillars feed on figs and papaya rather than milkweed, and the adults join the great mixed tiger-striped mimicry rings of the Brazilian forest.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are deep black with three faintly yellowish, transparent bands; the triangular patch at the base is the largest, while the transverse band across the middle is narrower and divided into five spots, the three lower ones dot-like. The hindwings are faintly yellowish and transparent, with widened veins and a black hind border, and four or five curved teeth.”
Named for Ilione, eldest daughter of Priam.

n202-3.name: Tigerwing
facts: An ithomiine tigerwing of the American tropics, one of the poisonous models at the heart of the orange-and-black mimicry rings that so many butterflies and even moths copy.
