The caterpillars feed on Solanum, the nightshades, and the adults gather in the forest understorey; Lucas's Antilles is doubtful for this Brazilian group.
Pauquet drew the wings extended beyond the cutter's frame; the pale wing tips of this specimen fall outside its box on the page.
Named for Narcaea, an epithet of Athena at Olympia.

n212-1.name: Elegant Acraea
facts: An acraea of the West African forest belt, tawny with a spotted border; acraeas are tough, slow, poisonous butterflies that bleed a yellow fluid when handled and that birds soon learn to leave alone.
Lucas used the name Zidora, but his own synonym, Cramer's Egina, is the older and correct one; Sierra Leone is right.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of all four wings is faintly yellowish. The forewings have at the apex a triangular black space on which sits a patch of fine pale tawny, rounded outwardly, sinuous inwardly and narrowed at its lower end; the hindwings carry a row of well-spaced black spots on the hind margin. The body is whitish beneath and black above.”
Named for Zidora, of uncertain origin; Cramer had earlier called this butterfly Egina.

n212-2.name: Euryta Acraea
facts: A forest acraea of West Africa with translucent forewings crossed by a pale band, white in the female and dull in the male, as Lucas described.
Linnaeus named it Euryta in 1758 after the archer-king Eurytus; Lucas's Sierra Leone is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “In this species the wings are proportionally less narrow than in the preceding ones. Their upperside is a deep matt black with the hind edge cut by white and slightly sinuous. The forewings are crossed by two lines of faintly shining sulphur-yellow spots, the inner line of about six spots arching from the middle of the costa towards the inner angle, the outer of four spots midway to the apex.”
Named by Linnaeus for Eurytus, a king of Oechalia and famous archer.

n212-3.name: Thalia Actinote
facts: A South American relative of the African acraeas, now placed in Actinote; the Neotropical members of the group have the same tough bodies and slow flight and are equally poisonous.
Linnaeus named it Thalia in 1758 after the Muse; Lucas's Guiana and Brazil are correct.
Named by Linnaeus for Thalia, the Muse of comedy and one of the Graces.

n214-1.name: Vibilia Longwing
facts: A longwing of the genus Eueides, close relatives of Heliconius that share their passion-vine caterpillars and tiger colours but not their pollen feeding.
Godart named it in 1819 for Vibilia, the Roman goddess of travellers who had lost their way; Lucas's Brazil is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of the hindwings is dark brown at the base and along the hind edge, and crossed between these by a broad curved band of tawny or cherry red, toothed outwardly and marked in the middle with a few black dots; in the male this band just reaches the forewings, in the female it rises much higher and is divided into five oval spots.”
Named for Vibilia, the Roman goddess of journeys and of travellers who had lost their way.

n214-2.name: Julia
facts: An orange longwing of the American tropics that flies fast and straight in sunshine and lives for months; it is one of the butterflies seen drinking the tears of caimans and turtles for their salt.
The caterpillars feed on passion vines; Fabricius named it Julia in 1775, and the modern spelling Dryas iulia keeps the Latin i.
Lucas's Guiana and Brazil are within its range, which reaches Texas and Florida.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are blackish brown and crossed by a band, reddish white in the male and very white in the female, broader in her than in him, sinuous on its sides and cut by fine veins of the ground colour; it descends obliquely from the costa towards the hind angle, narrows greatly above it and folds inward to reach the inner edge. The hindwings are reddish in the male and reddish white in the female.”
Named by Fabricius for the Julian house of Rome. The modern spelling, Dryas iulia, keeps the Latin i.

n214-3.name: Juno Silverspot
facts: The caterpillars feed in dense gregarious swarms that can strip a passion vine bare, and in Brazil they are a pest of cultivated passion fruit.
The underside is spangled with silver, which gives the English name; Cramer named it Juno in the 1770s, and Lucas's Guiana and Brazil are correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are dark brown with ochre-yellow spots arranged thus: two longitudinal at the base, the front one shorter; two nearly round in the middle; five oblong, unequal and touching, forming a transverse band opposite the apex. The hindwings above are rust-coloured with rays or streaks and a dark brown marginal band.”
Named for Juno, queen of the Roman gods.
Lucas's Eva, from Surinam, is a tiger-patterned longwing, orange and black with yellow spots; it belongs in the tiger mimicry ring of the Guianas, but the species has not been fixed with confidence.
The name is Eve, the first woman; it is one of several plain names Fabricius scattered among the classical ones.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are black above, with the inner edge and two bands tawny: the front band runs from the base to about the middle of the surface, where it is deeply cleft, then descends curving and widening to near the anal angle; the outer band lies obliquely opposite the apex without reaching the edges. The hindwings are tawny above with black streaks and a broad, curved, crenellated black border.”
Named for Eve, the first woman.

n216-2.name: Humboldt's Longwing
facts: A tiger-patterned longwing named for Alexander von Humboldt, who returned from the Americas in 1804 with the collections that made Paris the centre of tropical natural history.
Longwings of this pattern belong to the great tiger mimicry ring of the Amazon, in which dozens of poisonous species share one livery; Lucas's Amazones is right.

Lucas, 1835: “The male is a vivid tawny above; the female a light tawny, a little darkened towards the base of the forewings. These have a black, slightly concave hind edge, and their apex shows from that edge to the middle of the costa a large triangular black space mostly filled by an oblique tawny patch cleft behind. The hindwings are toothed and end in a fairly broad black border divided by a double row of dusky tawny spots.”
Named for Alexander von Humboldt, whose travels in the Americas with Bonpland filled the cabinets of Paris.

n226-1.name: Scarce Bamboo Page
facts: A longwing whose wings are panelled with translucent celadon green; it flies high in the forest canopy of the American tropics and comes down to drink at wet sand and to feed on lantana.
Linnaeus named it Dido in 1763, after the queen of Carthage; the same species appears again on plate 67 under Linnaeus's other name, Steneles.
The caterpillars feed on passion vines, but unlike Heliconius the adults do not gather pollen.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are toothed and black above. The forewings have two bands of celadon green, one longitudinal, one transverse: the first, from the base, is lance-shaped and reaches the disc, keeping nearer the front edge than the inner; the second, broader and strongly interrupted, is made of five unequal oblong spots, and the costa carries a line of three or four small whitish-green spots from its middle to the apex.”
Named for Dido, queen of Carthage, who loved and lost Aeneas. Linnaeus gave the name in 1767.
Cethosia lamarckii is a lacewing of Timor and the Lesser Sunda Islands, named by Godart in 1819 for Lamarck, whose lectures at the Paris museum Lucas would have attended.
Lucas's New Holland is wrong; the species does not reach Australia, though its relatives do.
Named for Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, who coined the word invertebrate and whose lectures shaped Lucas's generation of naturalists.
A lacewing of Java named by Godart for Leschenault de la Tour, the botanist who collected there for the Paris museum between 1803 and 1806.
Lacewings, Cethosia, take their name from the fine scalloped and lace-edged margins of the wings, clear in this figure; their caterpillars feed on passion vines and are poisonous.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are nearly round and toothed. Their upperside is velvet black with a violet gleam, and a broad terminal band of ochre yellow, repeated beneath, formed of closely set wedge-shaped spots. Beneath, each wing is rust-coloured and drawn thus: between base and middle, three transverse bands of greyish green cut lengthwise by black lines, then a series of small spots parallel to the terminal band.”
Named for Jean-Baptiste Leschenault de la Tour, botanist of the Baudin expedition, who collected in Java.

n228-1.name: Orange Lacewing
facts: A lacewing of northern Australia and the Indonesian islands, orange with a black lace edging; the caterpillars feed in groups on Adenia, a relative of the passion vine, and the adults are distasteful to birds.
Cramer named it Penthesilea in the 1770s after the Amazon queen; Lucas's Java is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are tawny above with a blackish terminal band divided by a run of whitish crescents concave outwardly. Opposite the apex of the forewings is a large triangular space of bluish black joined to the border, carrying an oblique, sinuous white transverse band separated from the crescents by an arc of four or five white dots. The border of the hindwings is preceded inwardly by two rows of black spots.”
Named for Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, killed by Achilles at Troy.

n228-2.name: Red Lacewing
facts: A lacewing of New Guinea and northern Queensland, orange-red with a broad dark border cut by white crescents; Lucas's China is a mistake, since the species is Australasian.
Linnaeus named it Cydippe in 1763 after the heroine of Callimachus; the female, as Lucas noted, is brick-coloured where the male is bright.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are finely toothed and edged with whitish at the notches. The upperside is a vivid tawny in the male, a dark and faintly greenish brick colour in the female, with a very broad brownish-black border arched inwardly. This border casts a faint violet gleam and is entirely divided by two curved parallel lines of white crescents facing one another by their convex sides.”
Named for Cydippe, the Athenian girl tricked into marriage by an apple inscribed with a vow, in a tale told by Callimachus.

n230-1.name: Regal Fritillary
facts: A fritillary of the North American tallgrass prairie whose hindwings are almost black with white spots, unlike any other; it has vanished from most of its former range east of the Mississippi as the prairie was ploughed.
The caterpillars feed on violets and hatch in autumn to overwinter unfed; Lucas's Jamaica is a slip, but his northern America is right.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are tawny above with about fifteen black spots: the foremost linear and set transversely beneath the costa, which is itself black; the next forming a zigzag transverse band across the middle; the rest round, smaller and ranged in a line parallel to the hind edge, which is covered by a fairly broad black band toothed inwardly and divided in the male by tawny lunules, in the female by white dots.”
Idalia is an epithet of Venus, from Idalium in Cyprus where she was worshipped.

n230-2.name: Indian Fritillary
facts: The female of this Asian fritillary wears a dark forewing tip crossed by a white band, copying the poisonous plain tiger; the male, shown here, keeps the orange leopard spotting.
Daubenton had called it the Leopard of China, as Lucas records, and China is one of its homes; it ranges from Africa to Japan and Australia.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are yellowish tawny strewn with black spots above and end in a black border crenellated inwardly and carrying two rows of bluish lunules facing one another. Opposite the apex of the forewings is a large triangular bluish-black space crossed by an oblique, sinuous white band cut by the veins and marked below with two black dots. Daubenton called it the Leopard of China.”
Niphe means snowflake in Greek.
Fabricius's Juliana, from Amboina, is a large brown butterfly with pale hindwing panels carrying blue-pupilled eyespots; the species has not been fixed with confidence.
The specimen is the largest on its plate, and its forewing tips extend beyond the cutter's frame on the page.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are dark brown above with a broad transverse band of greenish white set between the middle and the hind margin. On the forewings the band is a double row of spots, the inner ones smaller and crescent-shaped, the outer oval and each charged with a large black dot; on the hindwings it is continuous, preceded outwardly by a string of lunules, with two black eye-spots having a bluish pupil and a yellow iris.”
Named for Juliana, a Roman feminine of the Julian name.

n232-2.name: Forest Mother-of-Pearl
facts: The pale pink and green of this figure is the mother-of-pearl sheen of Salamis parhassus, an African forest butterfly whose wings gleam like the inside of a shell and carry small eyespots on the hindwing.
Lucas gave no locality and the old name Aglatonice; the species flies in the forests from Sierra Leone to Kenya and Natal.
Named for Aglaonice, the Thessalian woman said to be the first female astronomer in Greece.

n234-1.name: Scarlet Peacock
facts: One of the commonest butterflies of the South American tropics, red-banded and black, found in every clearing and roadside from Panama to Argentina.
Linnaeus named it Amathea in 1758 after a Nereid; Lucas's Brazil and Guiana are correct.
Named for Amathea, one of the Nereids.

n234-2.name: Blue Admiral
facts: An admiral of Asia from India to Japan, black with a pale blue band; it sits on sunlit rocks and paths with wings flat and is quick to fly at anything that passes.
The caterpillars feed on greenbrier, Smilax, and the adults pass the winter in hiding; Lucas's China is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are greenish black above, a little shot, and crossed in the middle and towards the tip by a pale arched blue band, divided on the hindwings by a line of black dots. Beneath, the male is dark black from the base to beyond the middle, then wood grey strongly waved with brown, with a sinuous, almost marginal line of ashen atoms and a dirty white dot on the disc of the hindwings. Found in China.”
Named for Charon, the ferryman of the dead.

n234-3.name: Grey Pansy
facts: A pansy of South and South-east Asia, grey with rows of small eyespots along both wings; it flies low over grass and rice fields and settles often to bask.
Linnaeus named it Laomedia in 1758; Lucas's China and Java are both within its range.

Lucas, 1835: “Above, the wings are ash-coloured, a little reddish in the male, with three blackish, waved transverse lines towards the rear, between which runs a transverse row of eye-spots, six on the forewings and five on the hindwings, all but the two middle ones having the inner side of the pupil tawny; there are also some blackish waves near the origin of the front edge of the forewings.”
Named for Laomedia, a Nereid.
Godart's Sophronia, from Brazil, is a blue-green butterfly with black and white forewing tips; its modern identity has not been settled here.
Sophronia is the Christian maiden of Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered.
Sophronia means prudent in Greek, and is the name of the Christian maiden in Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered.
Cramer's Cloantha, from the Cape of Good Hope, is a tawny butterfly with a row of violet spots; it is one of the African pansies, Junonia, but the species has not been fixed here.
Cloanthus was one of Aeneas's captains.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are tawny above with a dark base and a curved, transverse hind row of six violet dots edged with black, much larger on the hindwings, whose middle shows a small black spot; the forewings have beneath the costa three short, parallel, slightly arched transverse bands of the same colour. Beneath, the wings are like the upperside but generally paler and a little pricked with blackish. Inhabits the Cape of Good…”
Named for Cloanthus, one of Aeneas's captains in the Aeneid.

Cramer's Orthosia, from Amboina, is a brown butterfly with three lilac eyespots on the hindwing; Lucas compared it closely with Orithya, and it is one of the Indo-Australian pansies, Junonia, though the species is not fixed here.
Orthosia is an epithet of Artemis.

Lucas, 1835: “This species differs from the one just described in that the origin of the costa of the forewings is brown instead of whitish; the eye at their inner angle is much larger and less round, flanked by two black dots inside the same iris; the upperside of the hindwings has no blue band but three lilac eyes, the front one larger and furnished with three white pupils.”
Orthosia is an epithet of Artemis, the upright one.

n246-1.name: Blue Pansy
facts: A pansy of Africa, Asia and Australia whose male carries a patch of brilliant blue on the hindwing; it basks on bare ground in the sun and rises to chase off intruders, returning to the same spot.
Linnaeus named it Orithya in 1758 after an Amazon queen; Lucas's China, Java and Bengal are all correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings above are a deep velvet black in the male and brownish black in the female, with two black eyes having violet-blue pupils and a reddish-tawny iris. The forewings, whose costa is whitish from its origin to the middle, have near the base four small oblique lines alternately tawny and bluish, and towards the tip three white streaks, the innermost broader and shorter.”
Named by Linnaeus for Orithyia, an Amazon queen.

n246-2.name: Dark Blue Pansy
facts: The same species as the figure below it: Lucas's Clelia, from West Africa, and his Oenone, from the Cape, are the two ends of one African butterfly's range.
The blue hindwing patch is the male's; the female is brown with a smaller patch.
Named for Cloelia, the Roman girl who escaped Etruscan captivity by swimming the Tiber.

n246-3.name: Dark Blue Pansy
facts: A pansy of savanna and gardens across Africa, black with a blue patch on each hindwing in the male; it basks on paths and bare soil and is one of the first butterflies a visitor to Africa sees.
Linnaeus named it Oenone in 1758 after the nymph who loved Paris; the caterpillars feed on Asystasia and other acanthus-family plants.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are yellow inclining to tawny above, with all the edges black. This colour spreads broadly at the base of the hindwings and sets off a patch of violet or lapis blue, of much the same shape and size as in the preceding species. The forewings have at the apex, where the black widens entirely, two transverse yellowish streaks, the inner one shorter.”
Named for Oenone, the nymph who was Paris's first love and who refused to heal him when he lay dying.

n248-1.name: Tropical Buckeye
facts: A buckeye of the American tropics from Texas to Argentina, brown with two eyespots on each wing; Lucas listed six earlier names for it, a sign of how variable it is from place to place.
Fabricius named it Larinia in 1793; the names Lavinia and Evarete, which Lucas cites from Cramer, are the ones used today.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of each wing is dark brown with two black eyes, their pupil bluish and their iris yellowish grey. These eyes are immediately preceded outwardly by a tawny line, more or less deep, itself preceded by a double waved marginal line of the same grey as the iris. The forewings have towards the origin of the costa two small tawny streaks edged with black, and between the two eyes an oblique band, sometimes…”
Named for Larinum, an ancient town of Italy.

n248-2.name: American Snout
facts: A snout butterfly, named for the long palps that project from the head like a beak; Lucas noted the sharp points of the wings but not the snout, which lies flat beneath the body in a set specimen.
The caterpillars feed on hackberry, and in dry years the American snout swarms in Texas in migrations of millions.
Godart named it for Cuvier, the anatomist who dominated the Paris museum until his death in 1832.

Lucas, 1835: “All the wings are blackish brown with a violet gleam running from the base to beyond the disc. The forewings have seven or eight white dots, one cut in two near the middle of the costa, the others in two lines parallel to the hind edge. The hindwings are unspotted on both surfaces, but their underside, entirely glazed with violet, shows two dark, waved transverse lines.”
Named for Georges Cuvier, the great anatomist of the Paris museum where Lucas worked; he died in 1832.

n248-3.name: Red Rim
facts: A black butterfly of the American tropics with a rim of vermilion across the hindwing; it flies slowly and low, and its caterpillars feed on the stinging noseburn, Tragia.
Fabricius named it Biblis in 1775; Cramer's Hyperia, which Lucas cites, is the name used today, and Lucas's Brazil is correct.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown on both surfaces, the outer edge of the forewings less deep. Parallel to that edge the hindwings carry a broad, curved, spotted band of vivid vermilion red, finely notched on its sides; beneath it appears again, but rosy white and a little narrower, accompanied by four red dots, three near the base and one towards the middle of the costa.”
Named for Thadana; Cramer had earlier called this butterfly Hyperia.

n250-1.name: Giant Charaxes
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are brownish black above with a common, oblique tawny band across the disc. On the forewings the band is spotted, cleft in front and marked below the cleft with a line of three small black dots; on the hindwings it goes no further than the disc, and these wings have a reddish dot at the apex and a double row of unequal violet-blue dots along the outer edge.”
Charaxes castor, the giant emperor or giant charaxes, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found throughout the Afrotropical realm below the Sahel.
Named for Pollux, the immortal twin of Castor; Cramer had already called the same butterfly Castor.

n250-2.name: Common Blue Charaxes
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blue-black above with two transverse hind rows of light blue dots and a quite terminal row of earthy yellow lunules. Beneath, the ground of all four wings is a faintly shining greyish brown; towards the base are black, waved transverse strokes lightly edged with bluish, followed by a winding transverse series of yellowish dots.”

Charaxes tiridates, the common blue charaxes, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Senegal, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo,…
Named for Tiridates, the name of several kings of Parthia and Armenia.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above with a tawny or yellowish band towards the tip of the forewings and a white band towards the tip of the hindwings. The band of the forewings descends from the costa to the inner angle and is made of tawny dots in the male and of large wedge-shaped yellowish spots in the female. The marginal band of the hindwings is preceded by a band of ashen blue carrying a curved row of eight…”
Charaxes eurialus is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found on Ambon Island, Seram and Saparua in Indonesia.
Named for Nisus, king of Megara, whose purple lock of hair held the fate of his city.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are brownish black above, with the front half of the hindwings and a large triangular space at the origin of the inner edge of the forewings a livid yellow. The forewings have nine round spots of the same yellow, two a little beyond the middle of the costa and seven ranged parallel to the hind edge; the hindwings have two rows of blue lunules, the marginal one ending at the anal angle in a tawny crescent.”
Charaxes (Polyura) pyrrhus is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae.
Named by Linnaeus for Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, whose costly victories gave us the phrase Pyrrhic victory.

n262-1.name: Silver-studded Leafwing
facts: Lucas, 1835: “In this species the tooth before the anal angle of the hindwings stands out more than the others, and in the female the end of the tail is shaped, so to speak, like a foot. The wings above are brownish black with a violet gleam, with a broad, sinuous band of pale ochre yellow descending from the middle of the costa to the inner angle of the forewings, which carry one or more dots of the same yellow at the apex.”
Hypna is a butterfly genus of the family Nymphalidae. It is monotypic, containing only Hypna clytemnestra, the jazzy leafwing, marbled leafwing or silver-studded leafwing.
Named for Clytemnestra, who murdered her husband Agamemnon on his return from Troy.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above, crossed obliquely in the middle by a band of violet-tinged white, narrower on the forewings than the hindwings. The hindwings have the lower edge tawny from the anal angle to the tail inclusive, with five violet dots, the three outer ones edged with black. Beneath, all the wings are rusty brown with a few black, curved transverse lines edged with bluish at the base.”

Palla decius, the white-banded palla, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Senegal, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, the Republic of the Congo, the western part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and northern Angola.
Named for Decius Mus, the Roman consul who rode into the enemy line to die for his army.

n264-1.name: Common Pearl Charaxes
facts: Lucas, 1835: “Above, the front half of the wings is white, passing to yellowish towards the costa of the forewings; the other half is rusty, with two transverse rows of large tawny dots and an intermediate row of blackish dots on the forewings, and the reverse arrangement on the hindwings. Beneath, all the wings are the yellow of a dead leaf, with a few brown, waved transverse lines pricked with bluish near the base.”
Charaxes varanes, the pearl emperor, Karkloof emperor, or pearl charaxes, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae, found in Africa from Saudi Arabia to South Africa.
Named for Veranes, a Persian prince mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus.

Charaxes mycerina, the mycerina untailed charaxes, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Nigeria, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Equatorial Guinea.
Lucas called it Nymphalis mycerina; the accepted name today is Charaxes mycerina.
Named for Mycerinus, the Greek form of Menkaure, builder of the third pyramid at Giza.

n266-1.name: Orion Cecropian
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are brownish black above with a longitudinal tawny band covering about the whole front third of the surface, then narrowing to end a little short of the hind edge; towards the tip of the front edge is an oval white spot set lengthwise. The hindwings are brownish black above with a dusky tawny edge. Beneath, all four wings are brown shaded with grey, with two darker transverse bands near the base.”
Historis odius, the orion cecropian, is a species of crescents, checkerspots, anglewings, etc. in the butterfly family Nymphalidae.
Named for Orion, the giant hunter placed among the stars.
Lucas called it Nymphalis rogerii; the accepted name today is Siderone marthesia.
Named for a M. Roger, the collector who supplied the Cuban specimen; Godart honoured many such correspondents.

n268-2.name: Malachite
facts: Siproeta stelenes (malachite) is a Neotropical brush-footed butterfly. The malachite has large wings that are black and brilliant green or yellow-green on the upperside and light brown and olive green on the underside.
Named by Linnaeus for Sthenelus, charioteer of Diomedes at Troy.

n270-1.name: Pointed Sister
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are blackish brown above with a common, oblique white band across the disc, rounded at its front end and sharp or nearly so at the other. Opposite the apex the forewings carry an orange spot, more or less round in the male and an inverted triangle in the female, always separate from the white band; at the anal angle the hindwings have a small tawny patch bearing two black dots.”
Adelpha iphiclus, the Iphiclus sister, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae.
Named for Iphiclus, the swift-footed son of Phylacus, an Argonaut.

n270-2.name: Cherubina emperor
facts: Doxocopa laurentia, the turquoise emperor or Cherubina emperor, is a species of butterfly of the family Nymphalidae, subfamily Apaturinae.
Named for Laurentia, wife of the shepherd who raised Romulus and Remus.

Lucas, 1835: “Above, the wings are blackish brown with a common, oblique white band across the disc, less divided on the hindwings than on the forewings. The forewings have towards the origin of the costa three transverse spots of rusty red framed in black and separated by bluish ash; the hindwings have at the anal angle a tawny patch marked with two black dots. Beneath, two rusty lines with a white line between them run parallel…”
Lucas called it Nymphalis gelania; the accepted name today is Limenitis gelania.
Named for Gelanor, an early king of Argos.
Named for Iapis, the physician who healed Aeneas's wound in the Aeneid.

n280-2.name: Blood-red Glider
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are a vermilion red, a little shot, above, with an almost terminal row of black dots, faint on the forewings and joined on the hindwings by an angular black line. Beneath, all four wings are a light tan brown with black hieroglyphs at the base, a common oblique rusty line across the middle and dark chevrons topped with violet dots at the tip. The body is brown above and yellowish beneath.”
Cymothoe sangaris, the blood-red glider, is a species of butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Central Africa.
Named for the river Sangarius in Phrygia, now the Sakarya in Turkey.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above, with a common discal band whose inner side is mostly white and whose outer side is slate blue, spreading in rays to the hind edge. This edge carries white dots, the inner ones oblong and set in an arched line, the outer ones on the notches. Beneath, all four wings are dark brown with two rows of marginal dots as above and a band of violet-tinged white.”
Named for Amasia, the ancient city of Pontus, birthplace of the geographer Strabo.

Lucas, 1835: “The upperside of both sexes is a smoky black, crossed between the middle and the hind edge of the hindwings by a tawny band divided along its whole length by a curved row of seven very black oval spots, all, even the double and smaller anal one, carrying a blue dot in the middle. In the male this tawny band is narrower and surmounted by a large, faintly shining lilac patch. Daubenton called it the Palatine.”
Named for Callisto, the nymph turned into a bear and then into the Great Bear.

n282-2.name: Common Eggfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The male is brownish black beneath, and shows towards the middle of each wing a white patch surrounded by a violet gleam and cut by the veins: round on the hindwings, oblong and oblique on the forewings, which carry a similar but much smaller patch at the apex. Lucas lists more than a dozen names under which earlier authors had described this variable species.”
Hypolimnas bolina, the great eggfly, common eggfly, varied eggfly, or in New Zealand the blue moon butterfly, is a species of nymphalid butterfly found from Madagascar to Asia and Australia.
Named for Lasinassa; Fabricius's coinage, one of a dozen names this variable species has borne.

n284-1.name: Blue-banded Eggfly
facts: Lucas, 1835: “Above, the wings are a shot black with a common, arched blue band across the disc, behind which run three strings of blue spots, the inner ones wedge-shaped, the outer lunulate and placed opposite the notches, which are edged with white on both surfaces. Beneath, the wings carry the same pattern, but the edge is brown, the band and spots bluish white, and the costa of the forewings is dotted and dusted with white…”
Hypolimnas alimena, the blue-banded eggfly, is a species of butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in the Solomon Islands, Indonesia, New Guinea and Australia.
Named for Alcmene, mother of Heracles; Linnaeus spelt it Alimena.

n284-2.name: Blue Diadem Butterfly
facts: Hypolimnas salmacis, the blue diadem, is a butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo, Angola, Equatorial Guinea, São Tomé and Príncipe, the DRC, Uganda, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya and…
Named for Salmacis, the nymph who merged with Hermaphroditus in her pool.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are black above; the forewings show two transverse bands of a deep colour inclining to reddish, the one at the base very broad, the one nearer the front narrower and rounded on its outer side. The hindwings have a single band of the same colour, narrow, a little sinuous on the inner side and rounded behind. Beneath, the forewings also show a narrow, slightly arched yellow band and a very narrow blue…”
Named for Condomanus; Fabricius's coinage of uncertain origin.
Named for Hydarnes, a Persian general of Xerxes who commanded the Immortals at Thermopylae.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with a violet-blue gleam, changing in the male and absent in the female. In both sexes the forewings have at the base a longitudinal line, in the middle a transverse band and at the apex an oblique dash of a green that looks more or less golden according to the light; the hindwings have a band of golden or bluish green along the outer edge. Beneath, the forewings are carmine red from their…”
Named for Clymenus, a name of several figures in myth, among them a king of Orchomenus.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are velvet black above with a shining orange band across the disc, a little curved and scarcely rising beyond the centre of the forewings. Beneath, the forewings are a shining blackish brown with the rear half of the costa violet grey and the disc yellowish and furnished with black hairs lying flat; the hindwings are brown faintly shaded with grey, with an arched transverse line of a few blackish dots.…”
Named for Antiochus, the name of the Seleucid kings of Syria.

n288-1.name: One-spotted Prepona
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with a common, oblique band of shining greenish blue across the disc, arched and interrupted near the costa of the forewings and ending in a point on the hindwings. Beneath, the wings are brownish with three transverse bands of pearl grey, a black dot at the base of each wing and a waved line of the same colour descending from the front quarter of the costa to the inner angle.”
Archaeoprepona demophon, the one-spotted prepona, banded king shoemaker, or demophon shoemaker is a butterfly belonging to the family Nymphalidae.
Named by Linnaeus for Demophon, son of Theseus and king of Athens.

Lucas, 1835: “Both sexes of Nymphalis Demophon closely resemble the female of Nymphalis Demodice on the upperside; but the male of the latter has the blue band surrounded by a broad violet gleam, ending in a point a little beyond the disc of the forewings instead of being interrupted and arched near their upper edge. Beneath, rather more than the front half of all four wings is greyish white.”
Prepona laertes, the shaded-blue leafwing or Laertes prepona, is a butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in large parts of Central and South America.
Named for Demodice, a figure of the tale of Phrixus and the golden ram.

n298-1.name: Beltrão’s Owl Butterfly
facts: One of the owl butterflies: the underside carries a huge eyespot that reads as an owl’s eye when the wings are closed.
Named for Inachus, the river god and first king of Argos.

Lucas, 1835: “The wings are black above with a common band of shining violet blue across the disc, which reaches almost to the root of the wings while losing its brilliance. The forewings have towards the middle of the costa an oblique white spot and towards the tip white dots in one row in the male and two in the female; the hindwings, whose notches are also white, carry a series of red dots along the hind edge.”
Named for Leontes, a king of Sicily in Shakespeare's Winter's Tale, or for the Greek name meaning lion-like.

n302-1.name: Menelaus Blue Morpho
facts: Another Trojan name from Linnaeus. The blue is structural: the scales are stacked like tiny Christmas trees and reflect only blue light.
The undersides are brown with eyespots, so a flying morpho seems to flash on and off.

Lucas, 1835: “The male of this species had been given by authors under the name Menelaus, the female under that of Nestor. The upperside of the male's wings is a brilliant azure blue with the whole outer outline black and the notches of the outer edge yellowish white; on the costa of the forewings are three small white spots. The female is a somewhat less vivid blue, with the hind margin broadly black and charged with a row of…”
Named by Linnaeus for Menelaus, king of Sparta and husband of Helen. He named the female Nestor, after the old counsellor of the Greeks.

n304-1.name: White Morpho
facts: A pale morpho whose white takes a faint pearly blue in the light. Named for Laertes, father of Odysseus.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings are slightly toothed and a pearly white on both surfaces. Along the hind edge the upperside carries a double string of black spots, larger in the female, where they are separated by a scalloped black line; in both sexes the front half of the costa of the forewings is covered by a black streak that widens into a hook behind the submarginal cell. Beneath, a transverse row of black eyes with a tawny iris…”
Named for Laertes, father of Odysseus.

Lucas, 1835: “The four wings above are velvet black, especially towards the base, with faint, slightly yellowish notches. The forewings carry a transverse band of fine blue that shines according to the light, much broader towards the base and divided in three by the veins; near the outer edge a longitudinal band of pale yellow crossed by black veins runs from the apex of the forewings to the anal angle of the hindwings.”
Named for Lycaon, the Arcadian king turned into a wolf by Zeus.

n306-2.name: coconut caterpillar
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The wings are very entire and dark brown above. The forewings, whose front edge is strongly arched, are crossed from the middle of that edge by a curved, slightly sinuous tawny band reaching the inner angle and sometimes continuing, though shorter, to the corresponding angle of the hindwings; this band is more or less cleft at its origin. Beneath, all four wings are paler and finely pricked with grey, with a small…”
Brassolis sophorae, commonly known as the coconut caterpillar, is a species of large butterfly in the family Nymphalidae. It is found in South America.
Named for the plant, Sophora, on which Linnaeus believed the caterpillar fed. It actually feeds on palms.
Named for Toxeus, a brother of Meleager killed at the Calydonian boar hunt.
Named for Nicaea, the city in Bithynia where the Christian creed was fixed in AD 325.

Lucas, 1835: “In this species the forewings are entire and a little transparent. Their upperside is dark brown, sometimes unspotted, sometimes carrying parallel to the hind edge a run of four or five dots, the second from the costa black in a grey ring, the others wholly bluish. The hindwings are a little toothed and end outwardly in a small blunt tail; their rear half is deep black with some twenty blue spots, most charged with…”
Pierella lena, the Lena pierella, is a species of butterfly of the family Nymphalidae. It is found in Suriname, the Guianas, Peru, Bolivia and Brazil.
Named by Linnaeus in 1767; Lena is a plain girl's name, unusual among his classical choices.

Lucas, 1835: “The forewings are a little transparent, dark brown on both surfaces, with a linear white band descending obliquely from the end of the costa to the end of the inner edge. The upperside of the hindwings has about the front half and the outer edge dark brown, and all the rest tawny or Spanish-tobacco coloured, with a very white band edged with blackish; between this band and the hind edge are two very black eyes with…”
Pierella nereis is a butterfly species from the subfamily Satyrinae in the family Nymphalidae. It was first described by Dru Drury in 1782 from Brazil.
Named for the Nereids, the fifty sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus.

n310-2.name: Long-tailed Skipper
facts: Lucas, 1835: “The body is a dusky blackish with a tint of silky green at the upper root of the wings. The transverse white line of the forewings is made of four or five spots, touching or merely separated by veins, and ends a little before the inner angle; the hindwings have four more white, diaphanous but very small spots, one adjoining the hind edge of the streak near its middle and three in a little line near the costa.”

The long-tailed skipper is a spread-winged skipper butterfly found throughout tropical and subtropical South America, south to Argentina and north into the eastern United States and southern Ontario. It cannot live in areas with prolonged frost.
Named for Orion, the giant hunter placed among the stars.
Lucas called it Hesperia versicolor; the accepted name today is Mimoniades versicolor.
Versicolor simply means of changing colours in Latin.
